fields.Front: List the defining properties of a weak entity type.
fields.Back: No key attribute of its own; cannot exist without its identifying owner; always total participation with the owner (double line); owner may have partial participation; has a partial key (dashed underline); drawn as double rectangle with double-diamond identifying relationship; can sometimes be modelled as a composite multi-valued attribute instead.

fields.Front: How is a weak entity drawn in Chen notation?
fields.Back: Double-outlined rectangle; its identifying relationship with the owner is a double-outlined diamond; its partial key has a dashed underline; the line to the identifying relationship is double (total).

fields.Text: A weak entity is drawn as a {{c1::double rectangle}}, its identifying relationship as a {{c2::double diamond}}, and its partial key with a {{c3::dashed underline}}.

fields.Back: The attribute(s) that distinguish weak entities within one owner (e.g. RoomNumber within a Building). The full key is owner key + partial key.

fields.Front: In the BUILDING HAS ROOM example, why is ROOM weak, and what is its full key?
fields.Back: RoomNumber is not unique across buildings; a room exists only in a building. Full key: (BuildingCode, RoomNumber). Cardinality BUILDING (1) HAS (M) ROOM.

fields.Front: Does an identifying owner have to have at least one weak entity?
fields.Back: No; the owner may have partial participation (a building may have no rooms recorded).

fields.Text: A weak entity always has {{c1::total}} participation in its identifying relationship (drawn as a {{c2::double line}}).

fields.Front: When might a weak entity be represented instead as an attribute of the owner?
fields.Back: As a composite, multi-valued attribute (e.g. Rooms(RoomNumber, FloorNumber, SquareMetres) on BUILDING) when it has few attributes and no relationships of its own.

fields.Front: What relationship was added to the BUILDING/ROOM example, and why does it favour making ROOM an entity?
fields.Back: TENANT (1) RENTS (M) ROOM; because ROOM participates in its own relationship, it is better as a (weak) entity than as an attribute.

fields.Front: What are the instructor's two tests for a weak entity?
fields.Back: (1) Its key is not really a true key: it only identifies the entity within its owner (room 24 exists in many buildings). (2) It cannot exist without the owner entity.

fields.Text: Instructor's analogy: a {{c1::cell}} cannot exist without the {{c2::spreadsheet}}, so it would be a weak entity.

fields.Front: Contrast Student takes Course with Building has Room using the existence test.
fields.Back: A student can exist without the course and a course without the student (ordinary relationship); a room cannot exist without its building (weak entity).

fields.Text: In TENANT RENTS ROOM the diamond is single because the tenant {{c1::does not own}} the room; only the identifying relationship with {{c2::BUILDING}} gets the double diamond.

fields.Front: What is the George Foreman joke about?
fields.Back: Foreman named all his sons George, so Name would fail even as a partial key within that family; for most families Name distinguishes dependents within one employee.

fields.Text: Dependent Name is only a {{c1::partial (weak)}} key: unique within one family, but another family may also have a son named {{c2::John}}.

fields.Front: Why is the instructor's student number a good example of a true key?
fields.Back: Nobody else will ever get her student number (it merely gained an extra zero over the years); likewise her Western user ID is unique to her. A room number is not like that.
